transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

When I have to sit and focus on these long claim files, my mind just checks out and I end up putting them off or staring at the screen instead of getting them done. It's really starting to hurt my performance at work, so I wanted to see if there's something going on.
Do you find it difficult to focus or pay attention in other areas of your life, such as during conversations, reading, or watching TV, or is it mainly when you're working on these claim files?

It definitely happens in other areas too, like how I easily get sidetracked by background conversations around my cubicle. I'm not entirely sure about reading or TV, but this drifting has been a pattern since elementary school, when my teachers used to write comments about me daydreaming in class.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting, feeling restless, or having an urge to get up and move around when you're supposed to be sitting still, like in meetings or at your desk?

Yes, absolutely. When I'm at my desk, I'm constantly bouncing my leg, clicking my pen, or shifting around because I feel really restless trying to sit still. During long team meetings, I'll even get up to grab water or use the bathroom when I don't really need to, just because I feel too antsy to stay in my seat.
Do you often feel anxious, worried, or overwhelmed, or is your main issue more about difficulty focusing and restlessness?

I do feel anxious about losing my job and overwhelmed when trying to organize my desk, but those feelings are caused by my work piling up. The core issue is definitely my mind constantly checking out and that physical restlessness making it hard to sit still. It really feels like the focus and fidgeting problems are what's driving everything else.

You mentioned that this pattern of drifting and restlessness has been a problem since elementary school, but has the severity or impact of these symptoms changed significantly over time, especially during adulthood?

I managed through school and college by cramming and relying on my memory, but things got much worse about 15 months ago when my job switched to a high-volume, metrics-driven workflow. Since that change, I've struggled to keep up, gotten written up twice, and missed out on a promotion. Now, I'm constantly anxious that I'm going to get fired if I can't get this under control.

Can you describe any periods in your life where your symptoms of inattention and restlessness were significantly better or more manageable, and what factors you think contributed to those improvements?

High school and community college were definitely much more manageable because I could get by just by cramming before exams and relying on my strong memory for big-picture concepts. My tendency to drift off or misplace things didn't cause major issues back then because I didn't have to sustain focus on repetitive, precise details. Once my job shifted to this high-volume, metrics-driven workflow, those old coping strategies stopped working entirely.
Do you think your difficulties with restlessness and fidgeting, or your problems with focusing and paying attention, cause you more trouble in your daily life and at work?

The problems with focusing and paying attention definitely cause far more serious trouble for me. While the restlessness and fidgeting are frustrating, it's my struggle to stay focused and finish my files that led to my write-ups and missed promotion. That lack of focus is what makes me constantly anxious about losing my job.
Have you experienced any symptoms of hyperactivity, such as feeling constantly 'on the go' or talking excessively, in addition to your restlessness and fidgeting?

No, I don't really feel constantly "on the go" or talk excessively at all. My physical restlessness is mostly limited to fidgeting at my desk, like bouncing my leg, clicking my pen, or shifting in my chair. It also just makes me feel too antsy to stay seated during long meetings, which is why I end up getting up to grab water or use the restroom just to move around.

Have you ever found yourself interrupting others during conversations, blurting out answers before questions are finished, or having difficulty waiting for your turn, which could be related to impulsivity issues?

No, I don't really experience those issues with interrupting others, blurting out answers, or waiting my turn. My main struggles are much more about staying focused and getting organized, rather than being impulsive in conversations.
Can you think of any situations where you might have acted on impulse, such as making reckless decisions or engaging in impulsive behaviors, outside of your difficulties with focus and restlessness?

I can't really think of any times where I've acted impulsively or made reckless decisions. My issues are much more about struggling to stay focused, getting easily distracted, and feeling physically restless or antsy. I've never really been someone who acts on impulse like that.

You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood but worsened with your job change; can you describe how your symptoms impact your daily life and relationships outside of work, such as with friends and family?

I haven't really noticed my symptoms affecting my relationships with friends or family too much. Most of my struggles and stress are concentrated on my work and keeping up with daily tasks like remembering appointments, rather than my social life.

Can you think of any times when you had to engage in activities that required sustained mental effort, like studying for a test or working on a complex project, and how you managed your focus and restlessness during those times?

In school and college, I managed by cramming right before exams and relying on my memory, but now I hit a "mental wall" with long files and avoid them by checking email or getting coffee. To deal with the restlessness during those long tasks, I constantly bounce my leg, click my pen, or get up to grab water during meetings just to move around.

Can you think of any times when you felt like you were able to focus and avoid distractions, but still experienced significant restlessness or fidgeting, or was it usually the case that when you were able to focus, the restlessness decreased?

I'm not entirely sure or haven't paid close enough attention to whether the fidgeting goes away on the rare occasions I can actually focus. But when I'm at my desk trying to get through my files, the leg bouncing and pen clicking seem to happen constantly anyway.
Can you recall any instances where you exhibited excessive running, climbing, or other physical activity in inappropriate situations, such as in a quiet office setting or during a meeting?

I don't recall ever doing things like running or climbing in inappropriate situations. I do get really antsy and fidgety at my desk, or feel the need to get up and walk around, but it has never been anything extreme like that.

You've described significant difficulties with focus and restlessness, but can you clarify if you've ever experienced a period where your symptoms of inattention were more prominent than your restlessness, or vice versa, to help understand the balance between these issues?

I'm not really sure if there were ever distinct periods where one was worse than the other. The focus and daydreaming issues have felt pretty constant since childhood, while the restlessness and fidgeting are things I mostly notice when I'm forced to sit still at my desk for a long time. I don't really think of them as separate phases.

Do you think your difficulties with inattention, such as daydreaming and struggling to focus, have always been a more significant problem for you than your restlessness and fidgeting, or have there been times when the restlessness was the more dominant issue?

Yes, the daydreaming and focus problems have definitely always been the much bigger and more dominant issue for me, dating all the way back to elementary school. While I do get restless and fidget at my desk, those physical symptoms have never been nearly as disruptive as my mental struggles with focusing, organizing, and actually getting my work done.

To confirm, you feel that your difficulties with focus and attention have always been the primary issue for you, rather than the restlessness and fidgeting, which have been more of a secondary concern, is that correct?

Yes, that's absolutely correct. The issues with focus, getting overwhelmed by long files, and my mind constantly drifting are definitely the primary problems causing me major trouble at work. While I do fidget, bounce my leg, and feel antsy in meetings, those physical things feel much more secondary and manageable compared to the mental block I hit when trying to concentrate.

You've consistently mentioned that your focus and attention issues are the primary problems, but can you estimate how often your restlessness and fidgeting occur when you're not trying to focus on a specific task, such as during leisure activities or relaxing with family and friends?

I'm not entirely sure, as I haven't really noticed it happening much when I'm relaxing with family or friends. The restlessness and fidgeting mostly stand out when I am forced to sit still at my desk for work. Outside of that environment, it doesn't really seem to be an issue.

You've emphasized that your focus and attention issues are the primary problems, but can you think of any situations where your restlessness and fidgeting might have caused more significant difficulties for you than your focus issues, perhaps in social or other non-work settings?

I can't really think of any situations in social or non-work settings where my restlessness or fidgeting caused significant difficulties. Those physical behaviors mostly happen when I'm trying to force myself to sit still and focus at my desk. Work is really where almost all of my struggles are concentrated.

Can you summarize how your symptoms of inattention, such as daydreaming and difficulty focusing, compare in severity and impact to your symptoms of restlessness and fidgeting, to help clarify which set of symptoms is more dominant and disruptive in your daily life?

The inattention symptoms are definitely much more dominant and severe, as struggling to focus, getting distracted, and putting off long files are what actively cause errors and threaten my job. While I do fidget and feel restless in my chair, those physical sensations are just annoying and don't really cause any direct harm to my career or daily life.
Can you think of any times when your restlessness and fidgeting significantly interfered with your social interactions or leisure activities, rather than just your work or academic tasks?

I haven't really noticed my restlessness or fidgeting causing any significant issues in my social life or leisure activities. It mostly seems to stand out and bother me when I'm trying to work or stay seated at my desk. Outside of that environment, it doesn't really interfere with things.

Have you ever experienced symptoms of hyperactivity, such as an inability to engage in activities quietly, that are not solely related to restlessness or fidgeting, which might help differentiate between your current symptoms?

I don't recall ever having trouble engaging in activities quietly. My restlessness is pretty much limited to the physical fidgeting, leg bouncing, and needing to get up and move around that I already experience at work.

Can you estimate the frequency or proportion of time spent on tasks where your inattention symptoms, such as daydreaming, significantly impair your performance, compared to times when your restlessness and fidgeting are the primary issues?

I'm not really sure of the exact proportion or percentage of time spent on one versus the other, as I haven't tracked it that closely. Both seem to happen a lot during my workday, so I can't really give you a precise breakdown.

Can you think of any situations where you felt like you were able to control your restlessness and fidgeting, but still struggled with inattention and disorganization, which might help clarify whether these symptoms are independent or intertwined?

I can't really think of a specific situation where I successfully controlled my restlessness while still struggling with my focus. Whenever I try to force myself to stop fidgeting, like keeping my leg still, it just makes me feel more internally restless and tense rather than helping me focus or organize my thoughts. Because of that, they feel pretty intertwined for me.
Can you think of any situations where you were able to focus and avoid distractions, but still experienced significant restlessness or fidgeting, and if so, how did you manage those situations?

I actually find it very hard to focus or avoid distractions when I am feeling that restless. Usually, when I'm fidgeting or feeling antsy, my mind is already drifting or I'm struggling to stay on task, rather than successfully focusing.

Can you recall any instances where you felt an intense urge to be constantly active, to the point where it was difficult for you to relax or engage in quiet leisure activities, which might indicate a level of hyperactivity beyond just restlessness?

No, I don't really experience an intense urge to be constantly active, and I don't have trouble relaxing or doing quiet activities. My physical symptoms are pretty much limited to the fidgeting and restlessness I feel when I'm forced to sit still at my desk.

Can you think of any times when you exhibited behaviors that could be considered impulsive, such as acting without much consideration for the consequences, which might help differentiate between the potential diagnoses?

I don't really struggle with impulsivity or acting without thinking. My difficulties are much more about struggling to focus, getting distracted, procrastinating, and feeling restless rather than making rash or impulsive decisions.
Have you ever felt like you were 'driven by a motor' or had an intense urge to be constantly moving, even when it wasn't necessary or appropriate?

No, I wouldn't say I feel like I'm "driven by a motor" or have an intense urge to be constantly on the go. While I definitely get restless and fidget in my seat at work, it doesn't feel like an uncontrollable drive to keep moving all the time.

Can you summarize how your symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity have impacted your daily life, and do you feel that one set of symptoms has caused more significant problems for you than the other?

My inattentive symptoms, like struggling to focus on long files, disorganization, and making errors, have caused the most severe impact on my life, specifically leading to being written up twice and missing a promotion. While I do experience physical restlessness like fidgeting and needing to get up during meetings, those symptoms are just annoying. It is definitely the inattention and lack of focus that are causing the most significant, high-stakes problems for me.
Can you think of any situations where you felt like your restlessness and fidgeting were more prominent than your inattention symptoms, and if so, how did you manage those situations?

During long team meetings, the restlessness definitely becomes very prominent, and I manage it by making excuses to get up—like grabbing water or using the restroom even when I don't need to—just to move around. When I'm at my desk, I cope with that antsy feeling by constantly bouncing my leg, clicking my pen, or shifting in my chair. Those are really the main times the physical restlessness takes over.
